Q3847510.summary: In this venerated icon the Virgin, veiled in deep blue with a star on her shoulder, holds the Christ Child on her arm against a gold ground; the Child, in a light tunic, raises his right hand in blessing and looks up toward his mother. Both now wear silver crowns, recalling the icon's solemn coronation in 1955. Long honoured as the patroness of Manfredonia, the icon is carried in procession through the city each year on 31 August.
facts: Legend says the icon was painted in Constantinople in the 5th century and brought to Siponto, but historians date the panel to around the 11th century; the first certain records date from 1327.
A fire in 1872 destroyed the lower part of the panel, and later restorations (1896, 1927, 1964) left it extensively repainted; it was restored again in 2010–2011.
It was solemnly crowned on 28 August 1955 by Cardinal Angelo Roncalli, the future Pope John XXIII.

Q3847510.notes: The 4th-century date in the source data reflects legend; the work should move out of the 1st–7th century range (c. 11th century). The Commons photo was taken during the 2008 procession; since 2002 a copy by Aronne Del Vecchio has been carried in procession, so the photograph may show the copy rather than the original panel.

cur:catacombs-mp-good-shepherd-octagon.summary: Within concentric painted octagons on a ceiling, the Good Shepherd stands between two trees, a sheep on his shoulders and a vessel in his hand, with sheep at his feet. The geometric frame turns the ceiling into a window onto the green pastures promised to the faithful.
facts: Commons places this painting in the Catacomb of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; an early photograph of the same ceiling appears in 'Monuments of the Early Church' (1901).
The Catacomb of Marcellinus and Peter preserves an unusually rich cycle of 3rd–4th-century paintings.
cur:catacombs-mp-good-shepherd-octagon.notes: The Good Shepherd is read as Christ in this Christian context; the date is approximate.

met:463587.summary: This is an early 20th-century reproduction of the shrine made to hold the Stowe Missal, an Irish Mass book. The face shown, with its large central crystal and gem-set cross, has four engraved figures in the spaces between the arms; at the upper left is Christ crucified, alongside the Virgin and Child, a bishop giving a blessing and a cleric with a book. The original shrine, begun in the 11th century and given this face around 1375, is one of the oldest Irish book-shrines, and the replica preserves its image of the crucified Lord for study.
facts: The Met classifies this object as a reproduction (Rogers Fund, 1911); the original shrine is in the National Museum of Ireland.

On the original, one face and the sides date from c. 1026–33, according to their inscriptions; the face with the Crucifixion was added c. 1375 for Pilib Ó Ceinnéidigh (Philip O'Kennedy), 'king of Ormond', and his wife Áine.
The manuscript it protected, the Stowe Missal, dates from the late 8th or early 9th century and is now in the Royal Irish Academy, Dublin.
met:463587.notes: A modern replica. The Met's date line ('original dated 1025–52') refers to the older parts of the shrine, but the face shown with the Crucifixion reproduces the c. 1375 refurbishment. y is set to 1375 to place the depicted design; the editors may prefer to date the object itself (c. 1911) or to exclude replicas.
